newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian fuel crisis exposes national decay.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian fuel crisis exposes national decay.

text.p: Piqued by the irony that Africa's leading oil producer cannot provide enough fuel for itself, industry experts are attributing an excruciating fuel scarcity in Nigeria to years of national malaise.
Fuel shortage is not unusual in Nigeria, which pumps two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil. But the current one has lasted longer than normal and has shown no sign of easing.
"This phenomenon did not just start today. The seeds have been there all the time and were waiting to germinate," said oil company executive Remi Akinsanya.
"They range from underfunding of the oil industry to mismanagement and our lackadaiscal attitude to work," he added.
Military ruler General Sani Abacha stepped in on Monday and ordered imports of fuel to normalise supplies within 48 hours.
Since January, there have been intermittent fuel shortages. They usually abate after two to three weeks, but the current crunch started in mid-May.

Many people thought the situation would normalise within weeks as usual but it has turned into severe hardship for Nigerians by crippling transport and forcing many businesses to scale back or shut down completely.

"The situation has really exposed Nigeria as a nation that cannot manage its resources for the optimum benefit of its citizens," wrote Tajudeen Bello, editor of the semi-official Business Times newspaper in his Periscope column on Monday.

No definite explanation has been offered by the authorities for the scarcity. But finance minister Anthony Ani, an accountant who has waged an anti-corruption war within General Sani Abacha's military government, seemed to have opened a can of worms last week when he blamed the oil ministry for it.

"Despite the huge amount allocated for the repairs of the refineries, we have found that these have not been repaired, the result of which is persistent shortage of fuel in Nigeria, the world's sixth largest producer of crude oil," charged Ani.
He said $440 million and $295 million were allocated to Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) in 1995 and 1996 respectively for projects including refinery repairs.
An angry oil minister Dan Etete disputed this in a statement in which he called Ani's remarks "a deliberate falsehood with intent to incite the Nigerian masses".
His aides say Ani's refusal to release money to the oil ministry and NNPC was the cause of the problem.
"Buck passing is a familiar Nigerian tactic for ineptitude," commented pro-democracy activist Roland Teidi.
But the slanging match has provided ammunition for opposition newspapers to hit at the government for the crisis.

"It is shameful and embarrassing that lack of accountability or indeed acts of impropriety have destroyed the supply and distribution network of fuel in the country, causing unspeakable hardship for our people," said the National Concord in a front page editorial.
Nigeria has four refineries with a combined capacity to process 445,000 barrels of crude oil daily, but which operate at a fraction of their capacity due to deteriorating facilities.
Reasons ranging from official corruption to inept management have been adduced for the inability to get the system to function properly.
The fuel crisis is bound to advance the argument that only a privatisation of the oil sector, Nigeria's economic lifeline, can reduce graft and make the economy work.
Any privatisation will be followed by sharp increase in pump prices, to a level probably nearer to those of the current black market -- five to 10 times the official prices.
Nigerians, weighed down by years of crisis and economic decline, have been too busy scratching a living to riot.
"This is unthinkable elsewhere and it is remarkable that people have taken it in their stride," said a Western diplomat.
The last real public demonstrations were at this time in 1994 when Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of an annulled 1993 presidential, was arrested for proclaiming himself president.
Since then the authorities have threatened to put down any demonstrations forcibly. The militant oil unions have been restrained by the continued detention of their leaders.
Experts warn the fuel shortage will make it more difficult for Nigeria to realise its forecast of growth in gross domestic product of 5.5 percent for this year compared with 3.2 percent last year.
"This may not be possible because the various production unit units may not have much to contribute to the GDP of the country," said Bello.

Several diplomats noted that this kind of fuel crisis had in the past preceded major political developments in Nigeria, such as Abacha's assumption of power in 1993 during the crisis precipitated by the annulment of the presidential vote.
